performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
question: How does a fixed bass make the violin’s movement above it feel more precarious?
intro: The finale starts with the solo violin over a held bass, then turns cautious steps into slipping and running. A remarkably quiet Sirocco passage removes the low strings before the opposing winds drive the conclusion.

sections.label: Breaking ice and solo link · approximate

sections.mNote: the full strings develop the preceding wind figures

cues.title: A moving violin, a held bass
cues.text: The solo violin keeps changing direction above a long F in the bass. The low note gives the music a fixed point while the solo line moves around it; the orchestral upper strings initially rest.
cues.evidence: Mutopia III bars 1–20 show the solo over a held F, with the accompanying upper strings resting. The report’s opening is relatively subdued before the change at 0:20: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

cues.title: Walking on ice
cues.text: The sonnet asks us to imagine moving cautiously on ice, slipping, falling and getting up to run. These changing actions occupy the finale before its account of competing winds. The score supplies the programme, rather than a later performance tradition.
cues.evidence: The original Italian winter sonnet and the score annotations identify these actions: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

cues.title: Motion above a quieter foundation
cues.text: The soloist’s running figures climb and turn while the accompaniment offers a less mobile foundation. Follow one layer at a time: the apparent rush comes from the violin’s note pattern, not simply from everyone playing faster together.
cues.evidence: Mutopia bar 51 is marked Correr forte; the upper-string accompaniment sustains while the basso briefly rests. The same-recording guide places the running episode near 1:04, shortly after the report’s strong rise around 1:00: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A violinist’s working world
cues.text: Vivaldi’s father Giovanni Battista was a violinist at St Mark’s in Venice and probably gave his son his first musical instruction. The concertos draw on a violinist’s practical knowledge of bowing, figuration and register, not only on the seasonal poems.
cues.evidence: The Pietà biography documents the father’s work at St Mark’s but qualifies him as likely the first to teach his son: https://www.vivaldichurchvenice.com/en/biography-of-antonio-vivaldi. That qualification is retained. The comment about instrumental knowledge concerns the score’s violin writing, not a claim that the father taught a particular passage.

cues.title: The bass falls silent
cues.text: In the Lento marked for the Sirocco, the low strings rest and the upper parts become much quieter. The missing bass matters as much as the reduced activity: listen for how little weight remains under the upper-string phrases.
cues.evidence: Mutopia III bars 101–119 give the Lento/Sirocco and nineteen bars of basso rest. The guide places this around 1:59; report levels fall as low as roughly −37 to −40 dB during 2:10–2:30: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two named winds
cues.text: Sirocco and Borea are named in the score and sonnet. The first passage gives way to the north wind and then to winds in conflict. Vivaldi changes tempo and texture as well as using rapid notes to make that contrast.
cues.evidence: The score marks Il Vento Sirocco at bar 101 and Il Vento Borea e tutti li Venti at bar 120. The sonnet names the winds: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351; https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996.

cues.title: The gusts become a conclusion
cues.text: The full strings develop the wind figures in F minor. The finale closes by intensifying material from the immediately preceding episode, rather than returning wholesale to the quiet opening solo.
cues.evidence: The source commentary identifies the closing tutti as a development of the preceding wind motive; Mutopia’s last seventeen bars show rapid tutti figures and the F-minor close. The guide gives about 2:56; the report remains loud through 3:05 before the final decay: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The pedal changes under the strings
transitions.how: The bass moves from held F to held C, turning tonic support into a dominant pedal. The orchestral upper strings join the soloist and then articulate shorter, cautiously repeated figures. A fixed bass still anchors the scene, but the harmony now feels less settled.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bar 21 moves the basso F to C and adds the orchestral strings. The guide places this at 0:20.5, matching the report’s strong 0:20 change: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: A falling tutti releases the running solo
transitions.how: After the downward figures labelled as a fall, the soloist begins short, running semiquavers. The accompaniment becomes a held upper-string support, with the basso briefly resting before its pedal returns. The scene changes through articulation and distribution of activity.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bars 48–51 mark Cader à terra and Correr forte; the guide starts the running region near 1:04. The report’s change near 1:00 and increased level support the broad placement, not an exact fall timestamp: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The orchestra interrupts the running line
transitions.how: The solo’s passage towards C minor reaches a tutti interruption. Brief fragments, rests and renewed solo motion replace the preceding continuous run. The dominant G remains important beneath these exchanges before the following slow contrast.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bars 85–100 show the tutti interruption, short figures and solo continuation; the guide places the group around 1:37–1:59. The report has changes at 1:36, 1:46 and 1:50: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The low strings withdraw for the Lento
transitions.how: The rapid C-minor episode gives way to a slower E♭-major passage. The basso rests for the whole Sirocco span, leaving the upper strings to carry its restrained phrases. Tempo, register and the loss of bass weight all contribute to the contrast.
transitions.evidence: The score begins Lento at bar 101 and has nineteen bars of basso rest. The guide gives 1:59 and the report’s strongest boundary is 1:58, followed by the extended quiet region: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: Rapid solo figures break the quiet
transitions.how: The slow upper-string passage yields to rapid solo figuration. Brief orchestral bursts repeatedly cut across it as the bass returns, and the harmony moves from E♭ towards F minor. The contrast is abrupt; it is not a gradual crescendo inside the Sirocco.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bar 120 labels Borea and all the winds; subsequent bars alternate solo runs with tutti repeated-note bursts. The guide gives 2:36; the report rises from about −36.6 dB at 2:30 to −18.2 at 2:35 and −13.1 at 2:40: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The interruptions become the closing texture
transitions.how: The repeated-note wind figures pass into the full strings. Instead of introducing another pastoral scene, the final tutti extends their rapid motion and directs it to the F-minor cadence. The soloist is absorbed into the collective finish.
transitions.evidence: The closing tutti is identified in the commentary and visible in Mutopia’s final bars. The guide gives 2:56 and the report a boundary at 2:56: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: III. Allegro; solo opening, basso pedals, bars 101–119 basso tacet, and final wind episodes. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: The solo violin moves over the long F bass; orchestral upper strings rest.
Upper strings join over the held dominant C.
Running solo over sustained upper-string support; the basso briefly rests.
Low pedal support resumes beneath the continuing solo passage.
Tutti interruptions and a solo link alternate in this region.
The Sirocco Lento removes the basso for nineteen bars.
Rapid solo figures alternate with short orchestral wind bursts; participation is intermittent.
The full-string wind figures drive the conclusion.

composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.
